title: I built a stock research engine that can't hide its losses: every call is timestamped and measured against SPY after 20 sessions
author: krmill2k

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
the 20 session check against SPY will flatter anything high beta. in a rising market a 1.5 beta pick beats SPY without the call being right about anything, so I'd score against a beta-matched benchmark or at least print the beta next to each result.

I'd also publish the withheld calls as a count. withholding on stale data is reasonable, but if it's invisible it becomes the one place a bad call can quietly disappear, which is the exact thing you built this to stop.

replies.author: Shishsmurf
replies.body: What’s an example of a beta matched benchmark to use instead of the spy? And would you use it for any beta above 1?

replies.author: krmill2k
replies.body:
Simplest version: don't use a different ticker, scale SPY by the stock's beta. If a stock has a beta of 1.5 and SPY is up 4% over the window, the "expected" move is \~6%. If the stock did 7%, the call added \~1%, not the 3% a straight SPY comparison would credit.

If you want an actual ETF, sector funds work well (XLK for tech, SMH for semis, etc.), and there are beta-sorted ones like SPHB (S&P 500 high beta) and SPLV (low vol).

And it applies to any beta, not just above 1. Low-beta names get the opposite problem — they look bad vs SPY in rallies and look great in selloffs without the call having anything to do with it.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: simplest is beta times SPY over the same window, so a 1.5 beta name has to beat 1.5x the SPY move. a sector ETF like SMH or XLK is the other common one and catches sector rallies beta misses. I'd apply it to every call, not just beta above 1, low beta names get unfairly punished in a rally too.

replies.author: krmill2k
replies.body:
Both fair hits, thanks. You're right that raw excess vs SPY rewards beta in an up tape — a 1.5 beta name clearing SPY in a rally isn't evidence of anything. I'm going to add trailing beta (estimated pre-call, so no lookahead) next to every scored call, plus a beta-adjusted excess return (stock − β × SPY) and a sector-ETF comparison. Raw vs SPY stays, just not alone.

The withheld point stings because it's correct — an invisible withhold bucket is exactly the hiding spot the whole thing is supposed to eliminate. Plan is to publish withheld counts with the reason (stale data, guardrail, etc.), timestamped like the live calls, and track what those would have done in a shadow ledger so you can see whether withholding is helping or just dodging. Appreciate the push.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: beta-adjusted excess is the right fix. next one to watch is overlap: ten calls scored over the same 20 sessions are mostly one bet on the same tape, so I'd show a per-week number next to the per-call one. if you ever want each call run as a dated paper trade instead of a score, that's what Quantradin does. I built it, free at quantradin.com.

comments.author: CODE_HEIST
comments.body:
what happens if a stock is halted, delisted, or missing a price on session 20? i'd define that now and keep unresolved calls visible rather than dropping them from the score.



also worth fixing the first eligible price after publication. a timestamped call can still get an unrealistically favourable entry if it uses a close that happened before the call was available.

replies.author: krmill2k
replies.body:
Good questions. The entry one is already handled: entry is the first regular-session open strictly after the publication timestamp. A call published pre-market enters that day's open; anything published after 9:30 waits for the next session's open. SPY and the sector benchmark are measured over the identical sessions, and the scorer rejects the result if they don't line up. Withheld calls go through the same scorer, with the decision time recorded when the decision is made.

Missing or bad data already leaves a call visible as unresolved rather than dropping it. But you're right that halts, delistings and acquisitions don't have explicit rules yet. Today they'd land in "unresolved" by default, not by design. Adding:

* Halted through session 20: score at the first trade after it reopens, flagged as adjusted; still halted after a grace window → stays unresolved and visible.
* Acquired: score at deal/final price.
* Delisted for distress with no tradable price: scored as a total loss for a long call.

Also moving symbol tracking to a stable ID (FIGI) so ticker changes and reuse can't break a call's history. Appreciate it.
